units.en: But the queen, long since wounded by a deep anxiety, feeds the wound in her veins, and is consumed by a hidden fire. Again and again his courage comes back to her mind, again and again the honour of his line; his face, his words, stay fixed in her heart, and her love allows her limbs no peaceful rest.

The next dawn was lighting the earth with Phoebus's lamp, and had cleared the dewy shadow from the sky, when, hardly herself, she spoke to her sister, who shared her every thought: 'Anna, my sister, what dreams terrify me and leave me so uneasy!

Who is this new guest who has come into our home? How noble his bearing, how brave his heart, how strong in arms! I really do believe, and it is no idle faith, that his family is divine. Fear exposes a low-born spirit. Ah, by what fates he has been tossed! What wars he told of, and endured to the end!'

'If it were not fixed and immovable in my mind that I would not wish to join myself to anyone again in the bond of marriage, ever since my first love cheated and deceived me by his death; if I had not come to hate the marriage bed and the torch, perhaps I could have given way to this one fault.

Anna — I will admit it — since the death of my poor husband Sychaeus, since our household gods were spattered with blood when my brother murdered him, this man alone has moved my feelings, and stirred my wavering heart. I know the signs of the old flame.

But I would sooner pray that the earth gape open to its depths for me, or that the almighty father drive me down with his thunderbolt to the shadows, the pale shadows of Erebus, and deep night, before I wrong you, Honour, or break your laws.
That man, who first joined me to himself, has taken my love away; let him keep it with him and guard it in his grave.' So she spoke, and filled her lap with welling tears.

Anna answered: 'O you who are dearer to your sister than the light itself, will you be worn away, alone and grieving, all through your youth, and never know sweet children, or the rewards of love? Do you really think that ashes or the spirits in their graves care about that?

Very well: granted that, until now, no suitors have moved you in your grief, not in Libya, not before that in Tyre; that you turned down Iarbas, and the other chieftains that Africa, rich in triumphs, breeds. But will you fight even against a love that pleases you?

Does it not occur to you whose lands you have settled in? On one side, the cities of the Gaetulians hem you in, a people unconquerable in war, along with the unbridled Numidians, and the inhospitable Syrtis; on the other, a land made desert by drought, and the Barcaeans, raging far and wide. Why should I even mention the war brewing from Tyre, and the threats from your own brother?'

'I truly believe that it was with the gods as our protectors, and with Juno's favour, that the Trojan ships held this course before the wind. What a city you will see rise here, sister, what a kingdom, from such a marriage! With the Trojans' arms marching beside our own, to what heights will Carthage's glory raise itself!

You need only ask the gods for their goodwill, and once the sacrifices have been favourably received, give yourself over to hospitality, and weave reasons for delay, while winter and rainy Orion rage over the sea, and the ships are battered, while the sky is unmanageable.'
With these words she set Dido's heart ablaze with a boundless passion, gave hope to her wavering mind, and broke down her sense of honour.

First, they go from shrine to shrine, seeking peace at every altar; they sacrifice, as custom demands, chosen sheep to Ceres the lawgiver, to Phoebus, to father Bacchus, and above all to Juno, who watches over the bonds of marriage.

Dido herself, loveliest of all, holds the offering-dish in her right hand and pours it between the horns of a gleaming white cow; or walks before the faces of the gods to the altars heaped with offerings, and begins the day afresh with gifts; and, gazing into the opened breasts of the victims, searches their still-breathing entrails for a sign.

Ah, how little the minds of seers know! What good are prayers, what good are shrines, to a woman already mad with love? All the while the flame is eating at her soft marrow, and the silent wound lives on beneath her heart.

Unhappy Dido burns, and wanders in her madness through the whole city — like a deer struck by an arrow, which some shepherd, hunting among the Cretan woods, has caught off guard and pierced from a distance, leaving the flying shaft in her without knowing it; she runs in flight through the forests and glades of Dicte, the deadly arrow still fixed in her side.

One moment Dido leads Aeneas through the heart of the city, showing him her Phoenician wealth and the city already built; she begins to speak, and stops in mid-sentence. The next, as the day fades, she calls for the same feast all over again, and in her madness begs to hear once more the sufferings of Troy, and hangs once more on the speaker's every word.

Later, once they have parted, and the fading moon in turn dims her light and the setting stars urge sleep, she lies grieving, alone in the empty house, stretched out on the couch he has left behind. Apart from him, she hears him and sees him, though he is gone; or takes Ascanius onto her lap, caught by his likeness to his father, and keeps him there, hoping she might somehow deceive a love she cannot speak of.

The towers, once begun, no longer rise; the young men no longer practise arms, or make ready the harbours and battlements that would keep the city safe in war. The work hangs interrupted: the huge menacing walls and the crane that once rose level with the sky stand idle.

As soon as Jupiter's own dear wife saw that Dido was gripped by such a sickness, and that concern for her reputation could no longer stand in the way of her passion, Saturn's daughter went to Venus with these words: 'What splendid glory indeed, what rich spoils, you two are winning (you and that boy of yours, quite the great and memorable pair of gods), if one mere woman has been overcome by the trickery of two gods!
And it has not escaped me, indeed, that, fearing our walls, you have held the homes of high Carthage in suspicion. But where will it end? Or what is the point now of such a contest?'

'Why do we not instead make a lasting peace and an agreed marriage? You have exactly what you set your whole heart on: Dido is burning with love and has drawn the madness right through her bones. Let us, then, rule this people in common, with equal authority between us; let her be allowed to serve a Trojan husband, and hand her Tyrians over to you as her dowry.'

Venus knew well enough that Juno had spoken with false intent, meaning to turn the kingdom of Italy aside to the shores of Libya instead, and answered her in turn: 'Who would be mad enough to refuse an offer like that, or choose to go to war with you — if only fortune follows through on what you propose?

But I am adrift, uncertain about the fates, not knowing whether Jupiter wants one single city for both Tyrians and the exiles from Troy, or would approve of the two peoples mingling, or of treaties joining them. You are his wife; it is right for you to sound out his mind by pleading. Lead on; I will follow.'

Then queenly Juno answered her like this: 'Leave that task to me. Now listen, and in a few words I will show you how what needs to be done can be achieved. As soon as tomorrow's Sun has made his first rising and uncovered the world with his rays, Aeneas and most unhappy Dido mean to go out hunting together into the forest.

While the huntsmen are busy, and their nets ring the glades, I will pour down over them a black storm mixed with hail, and set the whole sky ringing with thunder. Their companions will scatter and be lost in the darkness,

and Dido and the Trojan leader will find their way to the very same cave. I will be there, and if I can be sure of your goodwill, I will join them in a lasting marriage, and make her his own. This will be their wedding.' Venus, who had no wish to oppose her as she asked, agreed, and smiled at the trick that she had seen through.

But not so the Phoenician queen, unhappy at heart: she is never released into sleep, or lets the night into her eyes or her heart. Her anxieties redouble, and her love, rising up again, rages and surges on a great swell of anger. So she persists, and thus turns things over within herself in her heart:

'Well then, what am I to do? Am I, a laughing-stock, to try my old suitors again, and beg as a suppliant for marriage with the Numidians, men I have already refused so many times as husbands? Or should I follow the Trojan fleet instead, and obey the Trojans' every last order? Is it because they are glad to have been helped by my aid before, and gratitude for that old kindness stands firm among men who remember it so well?

But, even if I wanted to, who would let me? Who would take a woman they despise aboard their proud ships? Don't you know, alas, lost woman? Don't you see yet the broken oaths of Laomedon's race? What then? Should I run off alone, and join their crews as they sail away rejoicing?

Or should I go after them, surrounded by the Tyrians and the whole band of my people, and drive out to sea again those I could hardly tear away from the Sidonian city, and order them to spread their sails to the winds?'

'No — die, as you deserve, and put an end to your grief with the sword. You, sister, gave way to my tears, and it was you who first loaded me down, mad as I already was, with all this suffering, and threw me to my enemy. I was not allowed to live out my life, innocent, untouched by marriage, the way a wild creature does, free of troubles like these. The vow I made to Sychaeus's ashes — I have not kept it.'
Such were the great laments that burst from her heart. Meanwhile Aeneas, now determined to sail, was snatching some sleep on the high stern, everything already duly prepared.

In his sleep the shape of the god, returning with the same face, appeared to him and seemed once more to warn him thus, in every way like Mercury in his voice, his colouring, his golden hair, and the graceful limbs of youth:

'Son of a goddess, can you really sleep on, with things as they stand? Can't you see, madman, what dangers are closing in around you? Can't you hear the west winds blowing, fair for sailing? She is turning over treachery and dreadful crime in her heart, set on dying, and stirring up shifting tides of anger.

Won't you flee from here headlong, while flight is still possible? Soon you will see the sea churned up with ships, and fierce torches blazing, soon the shore ablaze with fire, if dawn finds you still lingering in this land. Come now, break off your delay. A woman is always a fickle and changeable thing.' With those words he vanished into the black night.

Then indeed Aeneas, terrified by the sudden vision, tore himself from sleep and drove his men to headlong haste: 'Wake up, men, and take your places on the rowing benches; quickly, loose the sails. A god sent down from high heaven, look, is spurring us on again to hasten our flight and cut the twisted ropes. We follow you, holy one among the gods, whoever you are, and joyfully obey your command once more. Be with us, come gently to our aid, and set kind stars in the sky above us.'

So he spoke, and tore his flashing sword from its scabbard, and with the drawn blade struck at the mooring ropes. The same eagerness grips them all at once; they snatch things up, they rush; they have already abandoned the shore, the sea vanishes beneath the ships, and, straining together, they churn the water to foam and sweep across the blue.

And now early Dawn, leaving Tithonus's saffron bed, was scattering fresh light across the earth. As soon as the queen, from her watchtower, saw the light beginning to whiten, saw the fleet moving off under matched sails, and realised the shore and the harbour lay empty, without a single oarsman, she struck her lovely breast with her hand again and again,

tore at her golden hair, and cried: 'Ah, Jupiter! Shall this man really go, and shall a foreigner have made a mockery of my kingdom? Will my people not get their weapons ready and follow from all over the city, and will others not drag the ships down from the dockyards? Go, quickly bring fire, hand out weapons, drive the oars!'

'What am I saying? Where am I? What madness is warping my mind? Unhappy Dido, is it only now that impious deeds touch you? This was the time to feel it, when you were handing him your throne. So much for the pledged hand and good faith of the man who, they say, carries his ancestral household gods with him, who carried his father, worn out with age, on his own shoulders!

Could I not have seized his body and torn it apart, scattered it on the waves? Could I not have put his men to the sword, or even Ascanius himself, and served him up at his own father's table? True, the fortune of that fight would have been uncertain. Suppose it had been.

Whom did I have to fear, since I was going to die? I would have carried torches into his camp, filled the decks with flame, wiped out son and father together with their whole line, and thrown myself on top of it all.

Sun, whose fires look down on every deed done on this earth; Juno, witness and go-between of these torments of mine; Hecate, howled to at midnight crossroads in every city; you avenging Furies, and gods of dying Elissa: hear this, turn on these wrongs the divine power they deserve, and listen to my prayers.'

'If that cursed man must reach harbour, must come to land, and if Jupiter's fates demand it so, if this is where the line is drawn, then still let him be harried by the war and weapons of a bold people,

driven from his borders, torn from Iulus's embrace, let him beg for help and watch his men die undeserved deaths; and even when he has surrendered to the terms of an unjust peace, let him not enjoy his kingdom, or the life he longed for, but let him fall before his time, and lie unburied in the middle of the sand.

This I pray, these are the last words I pour out, with my own blood. And you, Tyrians — hunt down his line, his whole race to come, with your hatred, forever; send this as a gift to my ashes. Let there be no love between our peoples, no treaties, ever.

Rise up out of my bones, some avenger, to hound the settlers of Troy with fire and sword, now, or in time to come, whenever the strength arises: I call on shore to stand against shore, sea against sea, weapon against weapon; let them fight, they and their children's children after them.'

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: at marks a sharp turn from the end of Book 3, where Aeneas finally falls silent and rests. While he sleeps, the queen does not.

notes.label: Wound imagery
notes.body: Love is pictured as a wound, as if from Cupid's arrow. The image of a wound that will not heal runs through the book and ends in Dido's real wound from Aeneas' sword.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Her suffering has already lasted all night, perhaps since the banquet in Book 1, so the book opens in the middle of her pain.

notes.label: Paradox
notes.body: A wound should be tended so that it heals; Dido instead feeds it, which shows that she is keeping her love alive even as it harms her.

notes.label: Fire imagery
notes.body: The hidden fire eats her away from inside. Fire is the book's main image for Dido's love, and it will end in the real flames of her pyre.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The hard repeated c sounds give a harsh, biting quality to the idea of being eaten away.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: multus is repeated at the start of two clauses, so the reader feels Aeneas' qualities returning to Dido's mind over and over.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The v sounds bind the man to his courage. Dido does not separate the two: she loves Aeneas for his virtus.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: verbaque spills over into the next line, so even the structure shows his words clinging on. infixi, "driven in", recalls the arrow and the wound.

notes.label: Ring structure
notes.body: The first sentence opens and closes with cura, enclosing Dido in her love-sickness. At the end, cura denies her body any rest.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: A calm, bright dawn is set against the dark night of Dido's mind. The world wakes refreshed; she has not slept at all.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Anna is a sister who shares Dido's every thought, which explains why her advice will carry so much weight.

notes.label: Understatement
notes.body: Literally "badly sane": the phrase warns the reader that Dido's judgement is already unsound before she speaks.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Aeneas is a guest, protected by the laws of hospitality. The word will return with bitter force when Dido feels betrayed by him.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three things rising in admiration: his looks, his courage, his skill in war. The breathless exclamations show how dazzled she is.

notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.body: Dido is right: Aeneas is the son of Venus. The reader knows what she does not, that this divine family is the cause of her suffering.

notes.label: Sententia
notes.body: Dido argues like a general: only cowards show fear, so Aeneas' courage proves his noble birth. A short, quotable maxim.

notes.label: Exclamation
notes.body: heu and the exclamations show that she pities Aeneas as well as admiring him, and his story of suffering has moved her.

notes.label: Anna
notes.body: Dido's sister and closest companion. In some versions of the legend Anna, not Dido, was the one in love with Aeneas; Virgil makes her Dido's confidante and adviser.

notes.label: Phoebus and Aurora
notes.body: Phoebus Apollo as god of the sun, and Aurora, goddess of the dawn: an epic way of saying that the next day had begun.

notes.quote: si … sederet … si non pertaesum … fuisset … potui
notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: Two "if not" clauses hold back the main verb. Dido builds her defences first, then admits in a single word, potui, that she could have given in.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two near-synonyms stress how firm her resolve is, or how firm she wants it to sound. The reader soon sees it shaken.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Marriage is described as a chain or yoke. Dido presents it as something binding, which is what she fears and desires at once.

notes.label: Personification
notes.body: Her first love is spoken of as a person who tricked her. deceptam … fefellit doubles the idea of betrayal, a theme that will return with Aeneas.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated t sounds stress her weariness of everything to do with marriage; the torch is the wedding torch that led the bride to her new home.

notes.label: Euphemism
notes.body: Dido calls her love a culpa, a fault or sin, before anything has happened. huic uni tries to make it small: just this one failing.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: A verb of physical collapse, "to sink beneath". Love is pictured as a force that overpowers her.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: miseri shows her continuing pity and love for Sychaeus, which makes her new feelings all the more painful to admit.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The murder is pictured through the blood on the family gods: a crime against the home itself, committed by her own brother.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: solus stresses that only Aeneas has moved her, which makes her confession more complete and more dangerous.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: Her heart is pictured as a wall already slipping, and Aeneas has given it the push. The run-on to impulit enacts the push.

notes.label: Fire imagery
notes.body: Her love for Sychaeus was a flame; now she feels its marks again. The famous line is a moment of painful self-knowledge.

notes.quote: vel tellus … dehiscat vel pater omnipotens adigat
notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two terrible alternatives, one from below and one from above, show how strongly she means her oath.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: umbras is picked up and expanded at once, so the reader lingers in the darkness of the underworld, where Dido will end the book.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: Dido turns and speaks directly to her own sense of honour as if it were a goddess. Breaking faith with it becomes a kind of sacrilege.

notes.label: Tragic irony
notes.body: Dido swears she would rather die than break her vow. She will break it, and she will die: the oath is a curse on herself.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: ille at the start of both clauses points emphatically to Sychaeus. She tries to hand her love back to him in his grave.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: Her speech ends not in resolve but in tears, which shows how weak her defences really are.

notes.label: Sychaeus
notes.body: Dido's first husband, a wealthy priest of Tyre, murdered for his money by her brother Pygmalion.

notes.label: Erebus
notes.body: The darkness of the underworld, here a name for the land of the dead itself.

notes.label: The almighty father
notes.body: Jupiter, whose thunderbolt (fulmine) was the classic punishment for those who broke oaths.

notes.label: Hyperbole
notes.body: Anna opens with lavish affection, loving Dido more than life. It disarms Dido before the argument begins.

notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: Anna asks questions, not commands, so that Dido seems to persuade herself.

notes.label: Echo
notes.body: Anna uses the same verb as the narrator in line 2 (carpitur): Dido is being eaten away either way, by love or by loneliness.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Anna stresses that Dido is still young, so a life of mourning seems a waste.

notes.quote: nec dulces natos Veneris nec praemia
notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Anna offers children and love, the two things a widow gives up. The appeal is to Dido's heart, not her duty.

notes.quote: id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos
notes.label: Dismissive tone
notes.body: Anna brushes aside the dead Sychaeus as mere dust. The tone is blunt and practical, the opposite of Dido's devotion.

notes.label: Concession
notes.body: "Let it be so": Anna concedes Dido's past refusals only to turn them against her.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: The repeated non sweeps through her past rejections quickly, so Anna can move on to her main point.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: One word sums up Iarbas' humiliation. The rejected suitor will return later in the book as a dangerous enemy.

notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: The key question: resisting unwanted suitors was easy, but this love is welcome. pugnabis makes it sound like a pointless war against herself.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: Enemies are listed on both sides, so Carthage feels surrounded and in need of a protector.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Anna exaggerates the danger to make Aeneas seem essential to Carthage's survival.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: Literally "without bridles": the Numidians famously rode without bridles, and the word also makes them sound wild and lawless.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Even the land is hostile, a desert empty for lack of water.

notes.quote: quid bella Tyro surgentia dicam germanique minas
notes.label: Praeteritio
notes.body: Anna says she will not mention the threat from Pygmalion, and so mentions it. It is a clever way to end on the most personal danger.

notes.label: Iarbas
notes.body: A North African king, said to be a son of Jupiter Ammon, who sold Dido the land for Carthage and wanted to marry her. Her refusal makes him an enemy.

notes.label: Gaetulians and Numidians
notes.body: Peoples of the North African interior. The Numidians were famous horsemen, later allies and then enemies of Rome.

notes.label: Syrtis and the Barcaeans
notes.body: The Syrtes were shallow, shifting sandbanks off the Libyan coast, feared by sailors. Barce was a city in Cyrenaica, to the east.

notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.body: Anna thinks the gods favour the match. The reader knows that Juno does support it, but only to keep Aeneas from Italy.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Auspices were signs read from birds before any public act. Anna presents the Trojans' arrival as divinely approved, like an official undertaking.

notes.label: Epic epithet
notes.body: The ships are "Ilian", from Ilium, Troy. Synecdoche (keels for ships) and the grand adjective give her argument an epic tone.

notes.quote: quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna
notes.label: Exclamation
notes.body: Anna's excitement builds through exclamations, painting a glorious future for Dido to imagine.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Anna already calls it a marriage. The word is placed at the start of the line, so Dido hears the idea she has resisted presented as natural.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Aeneas is presented as a military ally. Anna turns a love affair into a defence policy.

notes.label: Tragic irony
notes.body: The Romans would destroy Carthage. Anna's vision of the two peoples rising together is the reverse of history.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Carthage's glory is pictured rising like a building, which looks ahead to the building work that stops once Dido is lost in love (lines 86–89).

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Anna makes it sound easy: just a few prayers and some hospitality.

notes.label: Euphemism
notes.body: Anna dresses up love as the respectable duty of a host. The word hospitium will become bitter later in the book.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: innecte, "weave", suggests a deliberate plot or trap. Dido is to hold Aeneas back with a web of excuses.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The heavy d sounds suggest the force of the winter storms that will keep the Trojans in port.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three reasons in a row for Aeneas to stay, each one practical, so that delay seems only sensible.

notes.label: Fire imagery
notes.body: Anna's words act like fuel on the fire already burning in Dido.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three verbs show Anna's speech working in stages: passion, then hope, then the collapse of shame.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: pudor, which Dido invoked in her oath (line 27), is now undone. The verb comes last, so the line ends on its loss.

notes.label: Orion
notes.body: The constellation Orion, whose setting in early winter was linked with storms at sea.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The sisters begin correctly, with the gods. Dido is still trying to do things properly.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: pax deorum meant the gods' approval, but the word also suggests the inner peace Dido cannot find.

notes.quote: Cereri Phoeboque patrique Lyaeo, Iunoni ante omnes
notes.label: Climax
notes.body: The list builds to Juno, goddess of marriage, which shows what Dido is really praying for.

notes.label: Polysyndeton
notes.body: The repeated -que gives a sense of Dido trying every god in turn.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The same phrase as in line 16, where Dido swore never to enter such bonds again. Now she prays for them.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Dido performs the rites in person, at her most beautiful. ipsa shows how much she cares about the result.

notes.quote: candentis vaccae media inter cornua fundit
notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: A precise, ritual picture: the white victim and the libation poured between its horns. It slows the narrative down.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: A word for walking up and down: Dido is restless even in worship.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: She keeps offering more sacrifices through the day, as if she can force the gods to agree.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: inhians, "with open mouth", shows Dido staring hungrily into the victims. Their opened breasts mirror her own wounded heart.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: The entrails are still alive, a grim detail that links sacrifice and death and foreshadows Dido's own end.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: The narrator breaks in with heu. Seers who read the signs cannot see what is obvious: Dido is beyond help.

notes.quote: quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant
notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: Two questions with repeated quid stress how useless her rituals are.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: furor, madness, is one of the key words of the Aeneid. Dido is now described as mad with love.

notes.label: Fire imagery
notes.body: est here is from edo, "to eat". The fire consumes her from inside, down to her bones.

notes.label: Wound imagery
notes.body: The wound from line 2 returns, alive and hidden. The section closes the circle of the book's opening images.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The soft v sounds make the wound sound quiet and secret, matching tacitum.

notes.label: Ceres, Phoebus and Lyaeus
notes.body: Ceres was linked with law and settled civic life; Phoebus is Apollo; Lyaeus, "the releaser", is a title of Bacchus. The gods of a city's foundation and of marriage.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The verb opens the section in a heavy, single word: Dido's burning comes before her name, so passion defines her before anything else.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: infelix, "ill-starred", is Virgil's recurring epithet for Dido. It marks her out as doomed and invites the reader's pity from the start.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: urbe furens runs over into the next line, so her wandering spills across the line break just as it spills through the city.

notes.label: Madness
notes.body: furens is the language of madness (furor): Dido is not simply in love but out of control, a theme that grows through the book.

notes.label: Simile
notes.body: Dido is compared to a wounded deer, an animal that is hunted and helpless. The image turns her love into an injury that will prove fatal.

notes.label: Word order
notes.body: The arrow (sagitta) and its participle coniecta frame the deer (cerva), so the word order pins her in place just as the arrow does.

notes.quote: pastor agens telis liquitque volatile ferrum nescius
notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.body: The shepherd who wounds without knowing it stands for Aeneas, who does not yet realise what he has done to Dido. nescius is held back to the start of a line for emphasis.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated s sounds give a rushing, breathless effect to the deer's flight.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The simile ends on the arrow still fixed in her, and letalis ("deadly") looks ahead to Dido's death. The l sounds slow the line to a close.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: The repeated nunc divides Dido's days into restless phases, showing how she swings from one activity to another.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: ostentat means "shows off": Dido displays her city as a way of winning Aeneas, perhaps hoping that he will settle there rather than found his own.

notes.quote: incipit effari mediaque in voce resistit
notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Dido cannot finish a sentence. The broken-off speech shows her confusion and shyness in front of Aeneas.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: The doubled iterum shows Dido asking for the same story over and over, hungry for anything that keeps Aeneas near her.

notes.label: Madness
notes.body: demens repeats the idea of furens: her obsession with Aeneas' story is presented as a kind of madness.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Dido literally "hangs" from his mouth, a vivid picture of how completely she is absorbed in him.

notes.label: Atmosphere
notes.body: Virgil reuses a line from Aeneas' story in Book 2. The soft s sounds and slow rhythm create a quiet night, which contrasts with Dido's sleepless grief.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: sola and vacua stress her loneliness once Aeneas has left the room, even though he is only elsewhere in the palace.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: absens absentem places the two absent lovers side by side, and the double -que gives the sense of a vision she cannot shake off.

notes.quote: gremio Ascanium genitoris imagine capta detinet
notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: Dido clings to the child because he looks like Aeneas. Readers of Book 1 know that Cupid took Ascanius' form there, so the scene is doubly charged.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: infandum, "unspeakable", marks her love as something shameful or forbidden: she has sworn loyalty to her dead husband Sychaeus.

notes.label: Crete and Dicte
notes.body: Crete was famous for its archers and hunters. Mount Dicte, in the east of the island, was said to be where Zeus was hidden as a baby.

notes.label: Ascanius
notes.body: Aeneas' young son, also called Iulus, from whom the Julian family (and so Julius Caesar and Augustus) claimed descent. In Book 1 Venus had Cupid take his place to make Dido fall in love.

notes.quote: non coeptae adsurgunt turres, non arma iuventus
notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: The repeated non lists everything that has stopped, so the city's paralysis is built up item by item.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: coeptae reminds the reader that Carthage was being built with energy in Book 1. Now the work has stopped, and the contrast shows the cost of Dido's love.

notes.label: Personification
notes.body: The unfinished buildings "hang" in mid-air, just as Dido "hung" on Aeneas' words in line 79. Her state of mind is reflected in her city.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The walls are called "threats", but with no one building them they threaten nothing, an image of power left idle.

notes.label: Hyperbole
notes.body: The crane that once stood level with the sky now stands still, which makes the halt in work seem all the more striking.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: Dido's love is called a pestis, a disease or ruin, which presents it as something destructive and contagious.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Dido's good name no longer holds her back. fama, reputation, will become important later in the book.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Juno is called "dear" to Jupiter, an ironic title for a goddess whose marriage is famously quarrelsome, and who is about to scheme behind his back.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: Saturnia recalls Juno's descent from Saturn, an older and harsher generation of gods, which hints at her stubborn anger.

notes.quote: egregiam vero laudem et spolia ampla refertis
notes.label: Sarcasm
notes.body: Juno uses the language of military triumph mockingly: Venus and Cupid have done nothing more heroic than defeat one woman.

notes.label: Parenthesis
notes.body: The aside is heavily sarcastic. The grand language mocks Venus and Cupid for ganging up on a mortal.

notes.quote: una dolo divum si femina victa duorum est
notes.label: Juxtaposition
notes.body: una ... duorum frames the line, setting one woman against two gods. Juno makes the "victory" sound as shameful as possible.

notes.label: Rhythm
notes.body: The heavy d sounds and the pointed placement of dolo stress the deceit behind Dido's love.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Juno shows she understands Venus' fears, which makes her seem shrewd and sets up her offer as reasonable.

notes.label: Possessive
notes.body: Juno calls Carthage's walls "ours", reminding Venus that Carthage is her city.

notes.quote: sed quis erit modus, aut quo nunc certamine tanto?
notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: Juno ends with questions that make her seem weary of the conflict and ready to compromise, which prepares for her offer in the next lines.

notes.label: Cupid
notes.body: Venus' son Cupid, who in Book 1 took the form of Ascanius and breathed love into Dido when she embraced him.

notes.quote: quin potius pacem aeternam pactosque hymenaeos exercemus?
notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: Juno frames her offer as a question, which makes it sound friendly and reasonable rather than a demand.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated p sounds link peace with the marriage pact, and the near-pun on pax and pactus makes the deal sound neat and settled.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Readers know that Carthage and Rome will fight three wars. Juno's "eternal peace" is bitterly ironic.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Juno flatters Venus by telling her she has already won, so agreeing seems the obvious next step.

notes.label: Fire imagery
notes.body: The fire image returns: Dido "burns", which links back to uritur in line 68.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: Love is pictured as a poison or fever that has soaked right through to her bones: it cannot now be cured.

notes.quote: communem hunc ergo populum paribusque regamus auspiciis
notes.label: Balance
notes.body: Juno offers equal shares, but the people would be ruled from Carthage, which is her real aim.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: servire, "to be a slave", is a harsh word for a queen's marriage, and Phrygio is slightly scornful. Juno's contempt for both of them shows through.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Dido's whole people are to be handed over like property, a reminder that the gods treat mortals as bargaining pieces.

notes.label: Parenthesis
notes.body: Virgil tells the reader directly that Juno is lying, so we watch the rest of the exchange knowing that both goddesses are playing a game.

notes.quote: quo regnum Italiae Libycas averteret oras
notes.label: Purpose
notes.body: The aside states Juno's real purpose: to divert Rome's destined empire to Carthage.

notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: Venus answers question with question. Her courteous tone hides the fact that she is not really agreeing to anything.

notes.quote: si modo quod memoras factum fortuna sequatur
notes.label: Condition
notes.body: si modo, "if only", is Venus' escape clause: she agrees in principle, but only if fate allows it, which she knows it will not.

notes.label: Fate
notes.body: Venus pretends not to know Jupiter's will, though she heard it in Book 1. Her uncertainty is a polite fiction.

notes.quote: unam esse velit … miscerive probet populos aut foedera iungi
notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three ways of uniting the peoples, each more formal than the last, show Venus listing the possibilities without accepting any of them.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Venus puts the responsibility back on Juno: as Jupiter's wife, Juno can ask him herself. The short phrase is pointed.

notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.body: Two short verbs with no connecting word end the speech briskly, and the half-line leaves the moment hanging.

notes.label: Hymenaeus
notes.body: Hymen or Hymenaeus was the god of weddings, and his name was used for the wedding song and for marriage itself.

notes.label: Phrygians and Tyrians
notes.body: The Trojans are called Phrygians, after the region of Asia Minor around Troy; Dido's people are Tyrians, from Tyre in Phoenicia, where she came from.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: regia stresses Juno's rank as queen of the gods, and the phrase matches Dido's own status as a queen.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: mecum comes first: Juno takes charge of the plan herself, confident and in control.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Juno speaks like a general giving orders. Her confident, businesslike tone contrasts with the passion of the mortals she is planning for.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: The superlative miserrima is Virgil's own comment, slipped into Juno's speech: Dido is doomed, and the narrator pities her.

notes.quote: primos crastinus ortus extulerit Titan radiisque retexerit orbem
notes.label: Imagery of light
notes.body: The grand description of sunrise gives the plan an epic setting. The idea of the world being "uncovered" contrasts with the darkness that will hide the lovers.

notes.label: Storm imagery
notes.body: The storm Juno promises is dark and violent, an ominous backdrop for a "wedding".

notes.quote: dum trepidant alae saltusque indagine cingunt
notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: Juno pictures the hunt in motion, so the storm will strike when everyone is busy and scattered.

notes.label: Hunting
notes.body: The hunters will be trapping animals, but Dido herself is the one being trapped, which recalls the simile of the wounded deer.

notes.label: Onomatopoeia
notes.body: The hard c and t sounds suggest the crash of the thunder Juno will send.

notes.label: Darkness
notes.body: The companions will be hidden by darkness, an image of secrecy that suits the shameful nature of what follows.

notes.quote: speluncam Dido dux et Troianus eandem
notes.label: Word order
notes.body: speluncam ... eandem frames the two lovers, so the word order traps them in the cave together.

notes.label: Formal language
notes.body: Juno uses the formal words of a Roman wedding. The promise of a "lasting" marriage is ironic, as it will last only a few months.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: A short, final phrase: Juno announces the "wedding" bluntly, which makes it sound more like a trap than a marriage.

notes.label: Litotes
notes.body: Venus agrees by not refusing, which shows how reluctant and calculating her consent is.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Venus smiles because she understands Juno's scheme and knows it will fail. The goddesses' amusement contrasts with the tragedy waiting for Dido.

notes.label: Titan
notes.body: The sun, here called Titan because the sun god Helios (or Sol) was the son of the Titan Hyperion.

notes.label: Cytherea
notes.body: A title of Venus, from the island of Cythera off the south of the Peloponnese, near which she was said to have risen from the sea.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The opening at non sets Dido apart from the sleeping world described just before: everyone else rests, but she does not.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: infelix returns from line 68: the doomed queen of the first half of the book is now near her end.

notes.quote: solvitur in somnos oculisve aut pectore noctem accipit
notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Sleep is denied three ways, in her body, her eyes and her heart, so the sleeplessness seems total.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: ingeminant, "they double", shows her anxieties multiplying rather than calming in the night.

notes.label: Sea imagery
notes.body: Dido's emotions are a stormy sea, an image that suits a story of ships and sailing. Her love has turned into rage.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: Love itself "rages" (saevit), a verb used of wild animals and storms, so love and anger have become one.

notes.label: Deliberative question
notes.body: The present tense ago, where a subjunctive might be expected, makes the question sudden and urgent, as if she is speaking her thoughts aloud.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: inrisa, "laughed at", shows how much Dido fears humiliation. She once rejected these men, and now pictures them mocking her.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The proud queen imagines herself begging: supplex shows how far she has fallen.

notes.label: Sarcasm
notes.body: Dido's bitter irony shows her sense of betrayal: the Trojans she rescued are repaying her with desertion.

notes.quote: bene apud memores veteris stat gratia facti
notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The sarcasm continues: Dido means the opposite, that the Trojans have no gratitude at all.

notes.quote: quis me autem, fac velle, sinet
notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: Even the option of following Aeneas is closed off, as Dido answers her own question.

notes.label: Self-address
notes.body: Dido turns on herself as perdita, "ruined" or "lost". The self-address shows a mind divided against itself.

notes.label: Allusion
notes.body: Dido brands all Trojans as liars, recalling the king of Troy who cheated the gods. The heavy, five-syllable adjective gives the insult weight.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: sola is set against the crowd of cheering sailors, so the picture of Dido alone among the joyful Trojans is especially painful.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: revelli, "tore away", recalls Dido's flight from Tyre after her brother killed her husband: she cannot ask her people to uproot themselves again.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Sea and wind recall the dangers the Tyrians already faced. The pairing makes the idea of another voyage feel exhausting and impossible.

notes.label: Phoenissa
notes.body: Dido came from Tyre in Phoenicia (modern Lebanon); Carthage was a Phoenician colony.

notes.label: The Nomads
notes.body: The Numidians, the native peoples of north Africa around Carthage, among them Iarbas, whose offers of marriage Dido had refused.

notes.label: Laomedon
notes.body: An early king of Troy who refused to pay Apollo and Neptune for building the city's walls, and later cheated Hercules. His broken promises became a byword for Trojan treachery.

notes.label: Imperative
notes.body: Dido gives herself an order, as if she were her own judge passing sentence. The abrupt imperative cuts off all the alternatives she has just considered.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Dido believes she has earned death. Her guilt over Sychaeus has turned into self-condemnation, so the reader sees how completely she now blames herself.

notes.label: Euphemism
notes.body: Suicide is described as a cure for pain, which shows that Dido now sees death as a release rather than a punishment.

notes.quote: tu lacrimis evicta meis, tu prima
notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: The repeated tu turns Dido's anger on Anna. The accusation is unfair, since Dido herself wanted Anna's advice, which shows a mind looking for someone to blame.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The participle stands at the end of line 548, so Dido's madness is the last word before the burden of suffering is placed on her.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: The affectionate word sits in the middle of an accusation, which shows Dido torn between love for Anna and resentment.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two verbs of violence present Anna as an attacker. Calling Aeneas hosti, an enemy, shows how far Dido's feelings have turned.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: Two sentences open with non, setting out what Dido has lost: an innocent single life, and her loyalty to her dead husband.

notes.label: Comparison
notes.body: Dido envies the freedom of a wild animal, which lives without marriage or guilt. The image recalls the wounded deer of lines 68–73 and suggests a life outside human ties.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Dido's speech ends on her dead husband's name, so the reader is left with the vow she has broken.

notes.label: Hyperbole
notes.body: Virgil stresses the size of her grief, and rumpebat, burst out, makes it sound violent, as if her heart could not hold it.

notes.quote: Aeneas celsa in puppi iam certus eundi carpebat somnos
notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The scene cuts straight from Dido's sleepless despair to Aeneas asleep and calm. The contrast makes his peace of mind seem cold beside her torment.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: The repeated iam stresses that Aeneas is ready and his mind is made up, while Dido is still struggling.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Rite suggests that everything has been done properly, even religiously. Aeneas is shown as orderly and dutiful, which sharpens the difference between him and the disordered Dido.

notes.quote: vocemque coloremque et crines flavos et membra decora
notes.label: Polysyndeton
notes.body: The list joined by -que and et lingers on the god's appearance item by item, which gives the dream vision a vivid, solid presence.

notes.label: Metre
notes.body: The double -que makes line 558 hypermetric: its final syllable elides into the next line. The line seems to spill over, much as the vision floods into Aeneas' sleep.

notes.label: Sychaeus
notes.body: Dido's husband at Tyre, murdered for his wealth by her brother Pygmalion. After his death she vowed never to remarry (4.24–29), and her shame at breaking that vow runs through Book 4.

notes.label: Mercury
notes.body: The messenger god, son of Jupiter. His first visit (4.265–276) ordered Aeneas to leave Carthage; this dream repeats the command with fresh urgency.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: Mercury reminds Aeneas of his divine mother, Venus, and so of the destiny that goes with his birth. The address is respectful and pointed at once.

notes.quote: potes hoc sub casu ducere somnos
notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: The opening question is a rebuke, not a request for information. It makes Aeneas' calm sleep look like dangerous carelessness.

notes.label: Insult
notes.body: Mercury calls the hero "out of his mind". The word usually describes Dido's frenzy, so its use for Aeneas is startling and urgent.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three questions in a row build pressure on Aeneas, each pointing to something he is failing to notice.

notes.quote: illa dolos dirumque nefas in pectore versat
notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: Mercury presents Dido as a plotter. The pronoun illa keeps her at a distance, which makes her seem a threat rather than a person in pain.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: Dido's anger is pictured as a stormy sea, which suits the voyage ahead and suggests something too powerful to control.

notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: Another question as a command: fugis, flee, is a blunt word for the departure of a hero, which adds to the urgency.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The same root repeated in different forms, with the hard p and c sounds, drives home the need for speed.

notes.quote: iam mare turbari … iam fervere litora
notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: The repeated iam paints a sequence of horrors as if they are already happening, so the threat feels immediate.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The image of fire looks forward both to Dido's pyre and, in the curse, to the wars of Carthage and Rome.

notes.label: Interjection
notes.body: Short, clipped words in the language of everyday urging. The rhythm itself hurries Aeneas on.

notes.label: Generalisation
notes.body: The neuter adjectives make "woman" a thing rather than a person. Mercury dismisses Dido with a general sneer, and the line has drawn criticism from readers ever since.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: femina is held over to the start of line 570 and stands alone, so the scornful judgement lands with full weight.

notes.label: Atmosphere
notes.body: The god vanishes into darkness, which leaves the scene ominous and gives Aeneas' fear a sudden cause.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: Present tenses make Aeneas' reaction quick and vivid: he moves the moment he wakes.

notes.label: Imperatives
notes.body: A string of commands shows Aeneas taking control of his men, and the short phrases match the haste of the moment.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: Aeneas stresses that this is the second divine command, which presents his departure as obedience to the gods, not desertion.

notes.quote: sequimur te, sancte deorum, quisquis es
notes.label: Piety
notes.body: Aeneas prays to the god even without knowing exactly who he is. The prayer shows his pietas, his dutiful obedience to divine will.

notes.label: The Zephyrs
notes.body: The west wind, which would carry ships from Carthage north towards Sicily and Italy: the perfect wind for leaving.

notes.label: Aurora
notes.body: The goddess of the dawn. If daylight finds the Trojans still in harbour, Mercury warns, they will be seen and attacked.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: Speech gives way to action in the same line, and the vivid present eripit makes the movement sudden.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The adjective, held over to the start of line 580, makes the sword gleam like a thunderbolt, an image of power and decision.

notes.label: Symbolism
notes.body: Cutting the cables is a physical act of leaving: the ties that held Aeneas to Carthage are severed with a weapon.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated f and r sounds give the stroke a harsh, decisive ring.

notes.label: Polysyndeton
notes.body: Two verbs linked by -que ... -que, both starting with r, capture the frantic, all-at-once movement of the crew.

notes.label: Perfect tense
notes.body: The perfect, after a run of presents, makes the departure already complete: before we know it, the shore is abandoned.

notes.label: Hyperbole
notes.body: So many ships crowd the water that the sea seems to disappear, which shows the scale and speed of the departure.

notes.quote: adnixi torquent spumas et caerula verrunt
notes.label: Rhythm
notes.body: The heavy opening word and the rowing verbs give the line the steady drive of oars pulling together.

notes.label: Personification
notes.body: The goddess rises from her husband's bed, a calm, mythological picture that slows the pace just before the storm of Dido's grief.

notes.label: Framing
notes.body: The noun and its adjectives frame the line, so the bed encloses Aurora herself, a neat, ornamental word pattern.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The scene cuts to Dido watching from above. The single word regina reminds us of her status at the very moment she is abandoned.

notes.quote: albescere lucem vidit … classem procedere … sensit
notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three things she takes in one after another, the dawn, the departing fleet, the empty harbour, so the reader shares her slow, dreadful realisation.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Empty and without an oarsman say the same thing twice, which stresses the totality of her desertion.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: A traditional phrase for repeated actions, used here for Dido's beating of her breast, which makes her grief formal and intense, like a mourner's.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: Decorum, lovely, sets her beauty beside the violence she does to herself, which makes the scene painful to read.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: Dido's outburst begins with an appeal to the king of the gods, as if calling him to witness the wrong done to her.

notes.label: Contempt
notes.body: Aeneas is reduced to "the newcomer", a word that denies all their shared history and recalls that he arrived as a refugee.

notes.quote: ite, ferte citi flammas, date tela, impellite remos
notes.label: Imperatives
notes.body: Four urgent commands in asyndeton show Dido trying, too late, to act as a ruler; but no one is there to obey.

notes.label: Tithonus
notes.body: A Trojan prince loved by Aurora, the Dawn. She won him immortality but forgot to ask for eternal youth, so he grew ever older in her bed. His being Trojan is a quiet irony here.

notes.quote: quid loquor? aut ubi sum? quae mentem insania mutat?
notes.label: Rhetorical questions
notes.body: Three short questions in a row show Dido coming to her senses with a jolt, aware that her orders are useless.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: Dido speaks to herself in the third person, as if she were watching her own tragedy from outside. Infelix is the word most often used of her in the poem.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: Impia is pointed: Aeneas is famous for pietas, and Dido now calls his conduct its opposite. (The phrase could also refer to her own deeds, the broken vow to Sychaeus, which makes it more painful still.)

notes.label: Tense
notes.body: The past tenses look back to her mistake: she should have been wary when she shared her kingdom with him, not now.

notes.label: Exclamation
notes.body: Sarcastic en: the right hand was the pledge of a promise, and Dido mocks the trust she placed in it.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: The repeated quem lists the famous proofs of Aeneas' piety, carrying the household gods and his father, only to mock them.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: One word turns praise into hearsay: Dido now doubts the stories she once found so moving.

notes.quote: non potui abreptum divellere corpus et undis spargere?
notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: The violent verbs build a picture of savage revenge, which shows how far grief has turned to rage.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: Spargere spills over to the next line, like the scattered body it describes.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.body: The repeated non piles up her missed chances, each victim closer to Aeneas.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: The gerundive conjures the most horrifying revenge of myth, a son served to his father, which shows Dido's thoughts at their darkest.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The boy's name is held back to the start of line 602 and stands out, so the reader feels the shock of her imagined target.

notes.quote: faces in castra tulissem implessemque foros flammis
notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: The past unreal subjunctives describe what she could have done, and the fire imagery anticipates her own pyre.

notes.label: Polysyndeton
notes.body: Her imagined destruction sweeps up every generation, a foretaste of the curse on Aeneas' descendants.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The doubled pronoun, memet ... ipsa, insists that she would have died with them, so murder and suicide merge.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Dido calls on three great powers in turn, each in a longer phrase, so her prayer grows in solemnity.

notes.label: Onomatopoeia
notes.body: The word imitates the cries of the worshippers at night, which gives the invocation of Hecate an eerie sound.

notes.label: Imperatives
notes.body: Three commands to the gods close the section, so Dido speaks with the confidence of someone owed justice.

notes.label: Ascanius
notes.body: Aeneas' son, also called Iulus, ancestor of the Julian family to which Julius Caesar and Augustus belonged.

notes.label: Hecate
notes.body: Goddess of crossroads, magic and the underworld, worshipped at night at places where three roads met.

notes.label: The Dirae
notes.body: Goddesses of vengeance, who punish wrongs such as broken oaths and crimes against family.

notes.label: Elissa
notes.body: Dido's other name, perhaps her Phoenician name. Here she speaks of herself as dying, morientis.

notes.quote: si tangere portus infandum caput ac terris adnare necesse est
notes.label: Conditional
notes.body: Dido opens by accepting what she cannot change: fate will bring Aeneas to Italy. The condition makes the curse that follows sound reasoned, not wild.

notes.label: Contempt
notes.body: Dido will not name Aeneas. He is reduced to a cursed "head", a word used in formal curses and sacrifices.

notes.quote: si tangere … et sic fata Iovis poscunt, hic terminus haeret
notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three ways of saying the same thing build to the solemn image of a boundary stone, so Dido seems to accept destiny before she twists it.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: The "bold people" will be the Rutulians and Latins under Turnus in the second half of the poem, so the curse already points to future events.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Two near synonyms double the threat, which gives the curse a heavy, ritual sound.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: The cruellest part of the curse is separation from his son. Avulsus, torn away, is a violent word for a father's loss.

notes.label: Jussive subjunctive
notes.body: A string of subjunctives turns wishes into commands, each one a separate penalty in the curse.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The word is held over to the start of line 618, so the shameful deaths of his men strike the reader with full force.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: Peace is the goal of Aeneas' mission, yet Dido wishes him a peace that humiliates him. The word iniquae turns the reward into a punishment.

notes.quote: sed cadat ante diem mediaque inhumatus harena
notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: Dying young and unburied was the worst fate a Roman could imagine. The image of a body on the open sand ends the curse on Aeneas with a picture of total disgrace.

notes.quote: hanc vocem extremam cum sanguine fundo
notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Dido presents the curse as a final offering, poured out like a libation, and her blood seals it. Her death will give the words their power.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: Dido turns from the gods to her own people and to all their descendants, so the curse widens from one man to two nations.

notes.quote: nullus amor populis nec foedera sunto
notes.label: Legal language
notes.body: Sunto, an old future imperative, belongs to the language of laws and treaties. Dido legislates eternal enmity.

notes.quote: exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor
notes.label: Address to the unknown
notes.body: The second person verb is aimed at someone not yet born. Every Roman reader knew she was summoning Hannibal.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The hard f sounds give the threat a fierce ring and recall the torches she imagined carrying into the Trojan camp.

notes.quote: nunc, olim, quocumque dabunt se tempore vires
notes.label: Asyndeton
notes.body: Time words with no connectives stretch the curse across every age, so there is no point at which it will end.

notes.quote: litora litoribus contraria, fluctibus undas … arma armis
notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: litora litoribus and arma armis set a word against another form of itself, with waves against water between them, so the clashing words act out the clash of the two nations.

notes.label: Metre
notes.body: The line is hypermetric: the final -que runs on into the next line, so the war Dido calls for seems to go on beyond the end of her speech.

notes.label: Iulus
notes.body: Ascanius, Aeneas' son. The name Iulus links him with the Julii, the family of Julius Caesar and Augustus.

notes.label: Unburied
notes.body: The unburied dead could not cross the Styx into the underworld. One tradition said Aeneas vanished in the river Numicus and his body was never found.

notes.label: The Tyrians
notes.body: Dido's people, who came with her from Tyre in Phoenicia to found Carthage. The Romans called the Carthaginians Poeni, Phoenicians.

notes.label: The avenger
notes.body: Hannibal, who invaded Italy in 218 BC and beat Rome at Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae, before his final defeat at Zama in 202 BC.

notes.label: Dardanian settlers
notes.body: The Trojans, named after Dardanus, their ancestor. Colonos, settlers, looks forward to their new home in Italy.
